reject_reason: pilot-judged for C01; nothing for C02–C13

items.note: Author describes a palace room with carved stone niches that must have housed an important person in Paramāra times; floors now torn up.
items.gloss: I jumped and climbed some way inside and reached a room that must certainly have been the residence of some very important person in the time of the Paramāras. The walls had splendid cupboards of carved stone, in which everyday articles must have been kept. At some time those stone walls, doors and cupboards must have been painted in bright colours. But now the floors were badly torn up, where vagrants were free to spread filth.

items.note: Palace ruins left abandoned and about to collapse, though rooms and verandas survive in fairly good condition after centuries.
items.gloss: It had been left completely abandoned on the verge of collapse. 'Let it survive on its own, let it fall on its own.' Even after centuries, inside the rubble-filled courtyard its rooms and verandas were in quite good condition.

items.note: Palace once ringed by a high protective wall; author states neither the Centre nor the state protects it, and it is not among the state's four protected monuments.
items.gloss: This was a very stinging unawareness of history for any sensitive person; seeing it, we both descended sadly and, circling this palace once enclosed by a high protective wall, started back toward the temple. Neither the central government had felt the need to protect it, nor is it among the state government's four protected monuments; we learnt this later in this campaign.

items.note: Palace's roughly twenty-foot stone defence wall between two bastions is broken, with a cement frame, iron gate and private-property signboard citing khasra and ward numbers.
items.gloss: As soon as we turned left from one bastion, we saw another bastion straight ahead. In front of this bastion the present crowded settlement of Udaypur begins. But between these two bastions we saw something quite different and attention-grabbing. The old stone defence wall of the palace, about twenty feet high, between the two bastions was broken in the middle. A long, tall cement frame had been built, with a big iron gate on it. A signboard on the wall declared it private property, with khasra and ward numbers and some phone numbers.

items.note: Author argues that neglected archaeological sites could introduce new generations to their forebears and be a worthwhile income source; every ruin holds stories of the past.
items.gloss: The panchayats also do nothing. Whereas, preserving these, what a fine and income-yielding means this could be to introduce the new generation to their ancestors. Our past's stories are in them. India has experienced so much that the identification of every ruin and every mound will confront us with some truths of the past.

items.note: Author says no panchayat representative, official, teacher or citizen took any initiative for Udaypur's decaying heritage.
items.gloss: Even after so many years of independence, none of the elected panchayat representatives felt this was something to be better looked after. No one in officialdom drew up even a paper proposal and forwarded it. No school teacher saw anything whose word could be carried further. It did not occur to any citizen to take even a small initiative for Udaypur's perishing wealth.

items.note: Most local people think of nothing beyond livelihood and farming.
items.gloss: Most local people think of nothing beyond their daily bread and farming. Even those whose daily needs are better met than others.

items.note: Author sketches the town layout from the lanes and old gates; roads crossed at 90 degrees in the time of Udayāditya (author's reconstruction).
items.gloss: Wandering through narrow lanes of unplastered stone houses and ancient gateways on both sides, we returned to the temple. On the way we also sketched an outline of the original plan from the time of King Udayāditya. How these roads must have been made, crossing each other at 90 degrees.

items.note: A mutilated goddess figure on the temple's outer wall, about six and a half to seven feet above ground: head cut off, hands hacked, a foot damaged.
items.gloss: When I came near him, my eye fell on a statue of a goddess. About six and a half to seven feet above the ground on the temple's outer wall, it was one of countless sculptures, mutilated yet very beautiful, its head cut off. Its hands had been cruelly cut off. The beautiful foot of one leg was also cut.

items.note: Dr. Suresh Mishra's first-visit reaction to the temple's architecture, left neglected in poor surroundings.
items.gloss: Seeing the temple's architecture from afar, Dr. Suresh Mishra, visiting Udaypur for the first time, was dazzled. He had no idea that a 24-carat historic place existed in such grandeur so near Bhopal, left neglected amid a very poor setting by local indifference.

items.note: Author places the Paramāras (ninth to fourteenth century) in a period of intense temple-building across Indian dynasties.
items.gloss: The period from the ninth to the fourteenth century in which the Paramāras flourished in this region was a time when dynasties across India were doing excellent construction in their kingdoms. From the Cholas far in the south to the Chandellas of Bundelkhand, from the Chauhans in Rajasthan to the Pala kings in Bengal-Bihar, the precious heritage built by generations was shining at its peak.

items.note: Udaypur was no capital but a small border place of the Paramāras touching Kalachuri territory; became an important centre because of sandstone quarries.

claim.value: on the Paramāra frontier, 500 km from Dhar (as stated)

items.gloss: This was not even the capital of any state. It was a small place on the Paramāra border, five hundred kilometres from their capital Dhar, whose strategic importance was that it touched the Kalachuri dynasty's territory. Udaypur became an important centre on the border of both dynasties because there were sandstone quarries here.

items.note: Under the Paramāras Udaypur developed like a mini capital; its importance lay in a future Paramāra emperor, the prince Udayāditya, living there in youth.
items.gloss: Under the Paramāras, Udaypur saw itself developing like a mini capital. Its importance lay in this: a future emperor of the Paramāra dynasty lived in Udaypur in his youth. That prince was Udayāditya, whose coronation Dhara city once witnessed. The same Dhara city that was King Bhoja's favourite city.

items.note: Sandstone quarries are given as the reason Udaypur became an important frontier centre.
items.gloss: Udaypur became an important centre on the border of both dynasties because there were sandstone quarries here.

reject_reason: narrative of author's photo review; no citable evidence beyond signboard anecdote covered elsewhere

items.note: Author's tweets and 5 January 2021 Facebook post 'Udaipur Palace, Khasra No. 822, private property' questioned how a thousand-year-old palace could be private property.
items.gloss: I wrote: how can a thousand-year-old palace be someone's private property? But it is so. Three pictures of Udaypur in Vidisha district, 150 km from Bhopal, bear witness. Whatever was recorded on that signboard I made the headline of an article on my Facebook page, with the same three pictures. The title of that post of 5 January 2021 was 'Udaipur Palace, Khasra Number-822, Private Property.'

items.note: Locates Udaypur in Vidisha district, 150 km from Bhopal.
items.gloss: Three pictures of Udaypur in Vidisha district, 150 km from Bhopal, bear witness to this.

items.note: Author states population of about eight thousand and that thousand to twelve-hundred-year-old buildings survive substantially.
items.gloss: I wrote that in this settlement of eight thousand people, buildings a thousand to twelve hundred years old survive to a considerable extent even today.

items.note: Whole town survives on its old design, with walls, gates, temples, palace, tanks, stepwell, rooms and lanes of Paramāra architecture.
items.gloss: The whole town exists in a rough condition on its old design, where there are walls, gateways, temples, palace, tanks, stepwells, rooms, walls and lanes built according to Paramāra dynasty architecture. Passing through them it feels as though you have returned to the past and are touring the lost splendour of centuries ago.

items.note: Signboard text and description of the palace with high stone enclosure wall and bastions, a wall broken for a cement-and-iron gate.
items.gloss: Can any part of a thousand-year-old palace surrounded by a high enclosure wall of strong stones and bastions be someone's private property, one of whose walls has been broken to fit a cement and iron door, with a signboard hung on the old wall: 'Private property, Udaypur Palace, Khasra No. 822, Ward No. 141'.

items.note: Place is famous for the Nīlakaṇṭheśvara temple built by Udayāditya, a generation after Bhoja; the town's name is linked to him.

claim.value: Mahārāja Udayāditya, a generation after Bhoja

items.gloss: This place is famous for the Nilakantheshwar temple, which Maharaja Udayaditya, of the generation after King Bhoja, had built. The name of this town, Udaypur, is also connected with him.

items.note: Royal-family members were given command of distant important towns and military posts as training in governance; author compares Ashoka at Ujjain.
items.gloss: In that period other important members of the royal family were entrusted with command of important towns and military bases far from the capital. In a way this was part of family training in running the state. Just as before becoming emperor Ashoka was sent to Ujjain by his father Bindusara as governor of Avanti.

items.note: Author's conjecture: prince Udayāditya may have been sent to border Udaypur and drawn up its first major development plan.

claim.value: conjecture: Udayāditya may have planned the town's first major development

items.gloss: It is quite possible that prince Udayāditya was sent to Udaypur, on the border of the Paramāra kingdom, in his father's time. It may be that Udayāditya himself made the first major plan for developing this border town and began excellent constructions as per his dynastic tradition, which continued after he became king.

items.note: Author argues the walled town with a palace within a vast enclosure and bastions is unique in the area; the settlement may pre-date Udayāditya as a Paramāra garrison.
items.gloss: Otherwise such temples are in village after village, but a palace surrounded by a vast enclosure wall and bastions inside a town protected by a square fort has its outline only here in this region. This must certainly have been a settlement established before Udayāditya, where a Paramāra military contingent would be posted to guard the borders. Udayāditya's appointment awakened the fortunes of this settlement.

items.note: Dr. Suresh Mishra: not only the temple but the whole town needs to be preserved afresh.
items.gloss: Dr. Suresh Mishra said with regret that not only the temple, the whole town here needs to be preserved anew.

items.note: Many buildings, palaces and temples survive but are crumbling; the author says responsibility lies with 'us', not foreign invaders.
items.gloss: Many buildings, palaces and temples survive here, giving a splendid introduction to India's centuries-old architecture. If they are not saved, it is turning to dust before our eyes. Now no foreign invader is doing this destruction. We are responsible for it.

items.note: Stone quarries supplied the basic building material in abundance.
items.gloss: The stone quarries provided in abundance the basic material necessary for construction.

items.note: Besides the original Śiva temple, several older temples and stepwells survive.
items.gloss: Besides the original Shiva temple there are several other old temples and stepwells that survive only by a miracle.

items.note: Author says the town was not untouched by Islamic attackers, evidence being broken images in the temple, yet the temple retained its original form.
items.gloss: This town has not been untouched by Islamic invaders. Evidence of this appears in the temple itself, where images have been broken. It is surprising that even so this temple remained in its original form, and this town too.

items.note: Author claims it is the only place in the district that could be developed as a tourism centre for a full day's visit.
items.gloss: This is the only such place in the whole district that can be developed into a splendid tourist centre where people can spend a full day peering into their past.

items.note: Visitors come daily mostly for the eleventh-century temple and Mahādeva worship; photographing has become a ritual, few examine the carved details.
items.gloss: Every day people come to Udaypur from far away. Most come only to see the 11th-century temple, and only to worship Mahadeva. Coming out of the sanctum they look up amazed at the temple's architecture. Mobiles are with everyone nowadays, so taking photos has become a necessary ritual like offering flowers, so that they can circulate on social media. Only a rare one would want to go into the details of this wonder carved on stone.

items.note: Author describes villagers as cut off from the past, indifferent to the present and dependent on governments.
items.gloss: This is an altogether different world. Cut off from the past. Careless of the present. Not even hazy imaginations of the future. They depend on governments for every small and big task.

items.note: Author's 2019 letter to a Vidisha collector proposed a Kashi Vishwanath Corridor-style effort to put Udaypur on the tourism map near Bhopal.
items.gloss: In 2019 I had written to a collector of Vidisha district, in a letter, some suggestions and requests with a view to preserving the history surviving in this town. I had written that there is scope here: if some work is done along the lines of the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, Udaypur in Madhya Pradesh, quite near the capital Bhopal, could shine on the tourism map.

items.note: Author laments that a thousand-year-old town 150 km from Bhopal is left neglected by representatives and administrators.
items.gloss: Only a hundred and fifty kilometres away, right under the nose of the capital Bhopal, an entire old town, preserved in its thousand-year-old splendour, seems to be gasping. But the people's representatives and administrative heroes, who journey from gram panchayat to Parliament, have shamelessly left it like a dung heap until now.

items.note: Author reports green cloth sheets recently laid at street corners and villagers relaying news of a pīr appearing, per a maulvi (author's perspective).
items.gloss: At the corners, junctions, roads and walls of Udaypur's lanes, pieces of green sheets have recently been laid. Innocent Hindu villagers, citing some maulvi, reverently hand over the 'breaking news' of the appearance of some unknown pir (Rahmatullah Alaih).

items.note: Signboard on the palace wall names the claimed owners (Qazi Syed family); the author did not know who they were.
items.gloss: Dr. Suresh Mishra underlined that the signboard hung on a wall of the palace of Maharaja Udayaditya of the Paramara dynasty announces a new ownership: 'Private property, Udaypur Palace, Ward No.-14, Khasra No.-822, Qazi Syed Irfan Ali, Qazi Syed Mehboob Ali, Qazi Syed Ahmed Ali.' We did not know who these gentlemen were, where from, or since when.

items.note: Author's inference: Udaypur was a splendid square town with equal walls and a palace, so heirs of Bhoja lived there, namely Udayāditya, after whom the town is named.

claim.value: named after Udayāditya, a Bhoja heir (author's inference)

items.gloss: Udaypur could be part of a deep research project in which King Bhoja's town planning is an important subject. It has been a splendid town in a square shape enclosed by walls of equal length on all sides, the presence of a king's palace inside which shows that Bhoja's heirs must have been here, and that is Udayaditya, after whom the town is named.

items.note: A fort defence wall built on Udaypur's hill in Paramāra times is still visible, including on Google Maps.
items.gloss: In the time of the Paramāras a fort defence wall was also built on the hill of Udaypur, which is visible today in front of us and on Google Maps.

items.note: Remains of an unfinished rock-temple project cut into the hill like Ellora; sculptures still visible on the cut hill.
items.gloss: There are also remains of a project of a rock temple, cut out of this hill on the lines of Ellora, which remained unfinished. Sculptures can still be seen on the cut hill.

items.note: A building on the only narrow lane to the temple now bears a Jama Masjid board, with large iron and plywood minarets added so the mosque will be seen from afar.
items.gloss: But soon this will stop being visible because a Jama Masjid board has been hung on a building in the only narrow lane leading to the temple. Large iron and plywood minarets have been put like caps on its small minarets. Now not the temple but this mosque will begin to be visible from afar.

items.note: The temple built by Udayāditya is visible from five kilometres away on the approach road.
items.gloss: Those who have gone to Udaypur or live in this area know that the temple built by Maharana Udayaditya becomes visible from five kilometres away. As you proceed toward Udaypur from the main road, the temple's grandeur is worth seeing.
